titulo: 'The Open Boat' by Stephen Crane, Part Two

fuente.licencia: Dominio público (VOA, gobierno de EE. UU.)
fuente.nota: Text shortened by removing paragraphs; the sentences are unchanged.

parrafos: We continue the story of “The Open Boat” by Stephen Crane. As we told you last week, the story is based on true events. In eighteen ninety-six, Crane was traveling to Cuba as a news reporter. On his way there, his ship sank in the Atlantic Ocean. Crane climbed into the last remaining lifeboat.

Three men got into the boat with him. They were the ship’s captain, the cook and a sailor named Billie. For three days, the men steered the small boat through high waves along the coast of Florida. At last, they saw land. Here is Shep O’Neal with the final part of the story.

A long stretch of coast lay before the eyes of the men. Slowly, the land rose up out of the mountainous sea. The men could see a small house against the sky. To the south, they could see a lighthouse. Tide, wind and waves were pushing the lifeboat northward. The men thought someone on land would have seen the boat by now.
“Well,” said the captain, “I suppose we’ll have to attempt to reach the shore ourselves. If we stay out here too long, none of us will have the strength left to swim after the boat sinks.”

The men then exchanged some information. There was a great deal of anger in them. They thought: “If I am going to be drowned, why, in the name of the seven mad gods who rule the sea, was I permitted to come this far and think about sand and trees?”

The waves grew stronger. They seemed always just about to break and roll over the little boat. The coast was still far away. The sailor said: “Boys, the boat won’t live three minutes more, and we’re too far out to swim. Shall I take her to sea again, captain?”
The man stopped walking. He moved his hand in the air to wave at them. He saw them! Now he was running to the house.
The captain tied a cloth to a stick and waved it. Now there was another man on the shore. The two men waved their hands in the air, as if they were saying hello to the men in the boat.

Now, what was that moving on the shore? It was a bus – a hotel bus. A man stood on the steps of the bus and waved his coat over his head. The men in the boat wondered what he wanted to say. Was he attempting to tell them something? Should they wait for help? Should they go north? Should they go south?
The men waited and waited but nothing happened. The sun began to go down. It got dark and cold. They could no longer see anyone on the beach.

The sailor rowed, and then the reporter rowed, and then the sailor rowed again. They rowed and rowed through the long night. The land had disappeared but they could hear the low sound of the waves hitting the shore. This was surely a quiet night.

A night on the sea in an open boat is a long night. The sailor continued to row until his head fell forward and sleep overpowered him. Then he asked the reporter to row for a while. They exchanged places so the sailor could sleep in the bottom of the boat with the cook and the captain.
The reporter thought that he was the one man afloat on all the oceans in the world. The wind had a sad voice as it came over the waves.

Suddenly, there was a long, loud swishing sound behind the boat and a shining trail of silvery blue. It might have been made by a huge knife. Then there was another swish and another long flash of bluish light, this time alongside the boat. The reporter saw a huge fin speed like a shadow through the water, leaving a long glowing trail. The thing kept swimming near the boat. He noted its speed and power. The reporter wished the men would wake up. He did not want to be alone with the shark.

The reporter thought as he rowed. He was angry that they had come so close to land and yet might still die at sea. Then he remembered a poem that he had learned as a child. It was a poem about a soldier of the French Foreign Legion. The soldier lay dying in Algiers. Just before he died, he cried out: “I shall never see my own, my native land.” And now, many years after he had learned this poem, the reporter for the first time understood the sadness of the dying soldier.

Hours passed. The reporter asked the sailor to take the oars so that he could rest. It seemed like only a brief period, but it was more than an hour later, when the sailor returned the oars to the reporter. They both knew that only they could keep the boat from sinking. And so they rowed, hour after hour, through the night.
“Well,” said the captain, “if no help is coming, we might better try to reach the shore right away. If we stay out here much longer, we will be too weak to do anything for ourselves at all.”

The others agreed. They began to turn the boat toward the beach. The captain told them to be careful – that when the boat came near the beach, the waves would sink it. Then everyone should jump out of the boat and swim to the shore.
As the boat came closer to land, the waves got bigger and more violent. At last, a large wave climbed into the air and fell on the small boat with great force.
The boat turned over as the men jumped into the sea. The water was like ice. The reporter was tired. But he swam toward the beach. He looked for his friends.

He saw Billie, the sailor, in front of him, swimming strongly and quickly. The cook was near him. Behind, the captain held on to the overturned boat with his one good hand. Soon, the reporter could swim no longer. A current was carrying him back out to sea. He thought: “Am I going to drown? Can it be possible?”

But the current suddenly changed and he was able to swim toward the shore. The captain called to him to swim to the boat and hold on. The reporter started to swim toward the boat. Then he saw a man running along the shore. He was quickly taking off his shoes and clothes.

As the reporter got close to the boat, a large wave hit him and threw him into the air over the boat and far from it. When he tried to get up, he found that the water was not over his head, only half way up his body. But he was so tired that he could not stand up. Each wave threw him down, and the current kept pulling him back to sea.

Then he saw the man again, jumping into the water. The man pulled the cook to the shore. Then he ran back into the water for the captain. But the captain waved him away and sent him to the reporter. The man seized the reporter’s hand and pulled him to the beach. Then the man pointed to the water and cried: “What’s that?”

The reporter did not know all that happened after that. He fell on the sand as if dropped from a housetop. It seems that immediately the beach was filled with men with blankets, clothes and whiskey. Women brought hot coffee. The people welcomed the men from the sea to the land.
This lesson plan, based on the CALLA Approach, teaches the strategy, predicting, to help students understand the story of four men struggling to survive in a small boat on the sea.
titulo_es: “The Open Boat”, by Stephen Crane (part two)
resumen_es: The end of Stephen Crane’s story: after seeing the coast without getting any help and spending a long night rowing, the shipwrecked men try to swim to the beach, where a man rescues them.
nivel_motivo: The vocabulary is simple, but the literary narrative, with interior monologue, imagery and allusions, requires B2-level comprehension.

ideas_clave.idea: This second part recalls that the tale is based on Crane's own shipwreck in 1896 and that, after three days at sea, the four survivors finally sighted land.
Although a house and a lighthouse were visible, nobody came to help, so the captain concluded that they would have to try to land on their own before they became too weak.
The men felt furious at the idea of drowning so close to safety, and as the waves grew, the sailor warned that the boat would not last and suggested heading back out to sea.
People on the beach spotted them and waved, even from a hotel bus, but the men in the boat could not understand what these signals meant.
No help arrived, darkness and cold fell, and the sailor and the reporter took turns rowing through the long night while the others slept.
Rowing alone, the reporter felt utterly isolated and was frightened by a shark that kept swimming around the boat.
He recalled a childhood poem about a dying legionnaire who would never see his homeland again, and for the first time he grasped its sadness.
Exhausted, the two rowers relieved each other hour after hour, knowing that their effort alone kept the boat from sinking.
With no rescue in sight, the captain decided to head for the beach and told the men to jump and swim once the waves sank the boat.
A huge wave overturned the boat; the men swam in icy water, and the exhausted reporter was dragged back out to sea by a current.
A man ran into the water and brought the cook and then the reporter ashore, while the captain, clinging to the boat, sent the rescuer to the reporter first.
The reporter collapsed on the sand as local people arrived with blankets, clothes and hot drinks to welcome the survivors.
A final note explains that the story is used in a lesson plan to teach students the strategy of predicting.

resumen_modelo:
The text presents the second and final part of Stephen Crane's story, inspired by his own shipwreck in 1896. After three days at sea, the four survivors, namely the captain, the cook, the sailor Billie and the reporter, finally sighted the Florida coast. However, no rescue came, so the captain concluded that they would have to try to reach the shore by themselves before their strength ran out.

The men were outraged at the thought of drowning so close to safety. Moreover, the waves were growing, and the sailor feared the boat would soon sink. Some people on the beach noticed them and waved, even from a hotel bus, yet the men could not interpret these signals, and as night fell nobody came. Consequently, the sailor and the reporter took turns rowing in the dark and cold. Alone at the oars, the reporter felt completely isolated, was frightened by a shark circling the boat and, recalling a poem about a dying French legionnaire, understood for the first time the pain of never returning home.

Eventually, the captain decided to head for the beach and ordered everyone to jump and swim once the boat capsized. A huge wave overturned it, and the men struggled in icy water; the exhausted reporter was even pulled back by a current. Finally, a man on the shore rushed into the sea, rescued the cook and, at the captain's request, the reporter. Local people then welcomed the survivors with blankets, clothes and hot drinks. A closing note adds that the story serves as a lesson on the strategy of predicting.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The men had been in the small boat for a week when they saw land.
preguntas.cita: For three days, the men steered the small boat through high waves along the coast of Florida. At last, they saw land.
preguntas.explicacion: The text says they spent three days in the boat, not a week, before seeing land.

preguntas.pregunta: Why did the captain think they had to try to reach the shore themselves?
opciones: Because if they waited too long they would be too weak to swim.
Because the people on shore had told them to come.
Because the boat was already full of water.
Because the lighthouse keeper could not see them.
respuestas: Because if they waited too long they would be too weak to swim.
preguntas.cita: If we stay out here too long, none of us will have the strength left to swim after the boat sinks.
preguntas.explicacion: The captain fears that, if they wait too long, they will not have the strength to swim when the boat sinks. Nobody on the coast had spoken to them yet, and the text does not say the boat was full of water or mention the lighthouse keeper.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The sailor believed that they were close enough to swim to the shore.
preguntas.cita: the boat won't live three minutes more, and we're too far out to swim
preguntas.explicacion: The oiler says exactly the opposite: that they are too far away to swim there, and he suggests going back out to sea.

preguntas.pregunta: What was the man standing on the steps of the bus doing?
opciones: Waving his coat over his head
Shouting instructions through a megaphone
Running towards the lighthouse
Taking off his shoes to swim
respuestas: Waving his coat over his head
preguntas.cita: A man stood on the steps of the bus and waved his coat over his head.
preguntas.explicacion: The man by the bus was waving his coat over his head. Taking off his shoes is done by another man much later, in paragraph 21; the megaphone and the lighthouse do not appear in this scene.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: Why were the signals from the people on the shore frustrating for the men in the boat?
respuestas: Because the men could see that they had been noticed, but they could not understand what the people were trying to tell them: whether to wait for help or to go north or south. In the end, no help came.
preguntas.cita: The men in the boat wondered what he wanted to say. Was he attempting to tell them something?
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraphs 8 and 9 show that the gestures from the shore were impossible to understand and that, in the end, nothing happened: night fell and no help came.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 11 that means “defeated, was too strong for”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'defeated, took control of'.
preguntas.cita: his head fell forward and sleep overpowered him
preguntas.explicacion: “Overpowered” means defeated, prevailed over (es: venció, se impuso); sleep overcomes the oiler while he is rowing.

preguntas.pregunta: What frightened the reporter during the night?
opciones: A shark swimming near the boat
A storm with thunder and lightning
A large ship passing close to them
The cries of the injured captain
respuestas: A shark swimming near the boat
preguntas.cita: He did not want to be alone with the shark.
preguntas.explicacion: The reporter sees a fin and a glowing trail: it is a shark swimming beside the boat. There is no storm and there are no ships, and the captain is asleep.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 13 that means “a thin flat part that a fish uses to swim”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'the thin flat part on the back of a fish'.
preguntas.cita: The reporter saw a huge fin speed like a shadow through the water
preguntas.explicacion: “Fin” is the part of a fish used for swimming (es: aleta); here, the shark’s.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The poem the reporter remembered was about a soldier dying in Algiers.
preguntas.cita: It was a poem about a soldier of the French Foreign Legion. The soldier lay dying in Algiers.
preguntas.explicacion: The poem was about a soldier of the French Foreign Legion who was dying in Algiers, as paragraph 14 says.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: Why did the reporter only now understand the sadness of the dying soldier in the poem?
respuestas: Because he himself was now close to death, near his own land but possibly unable to reach it, so he could feel the same pain of dying far from home.
preguntas.cita: He was angry that they had come so close to land and yet might still die at sea.
preguntas.explicacion: This is an inference question: the reporter’s situation, about to die close to land, allows him to identify with the soldier who will never see his homeland again.

preguntas.pregunta: Which men kept the boat from sinking during the night?
opciones: The sailor and the reporter
The captain and the cook
The cook and the reporter
All four men in turn
preguntas.cita: They both knew that only they could keep the boat from sinking.
preguntas.explicacion: Only the oiler and the reporter take turns at the oars; the cook and the captain sleep at the bottom of the boat (paragraph 11).

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 20 that means “turned upside down”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'turned upside down'.
preguntas.cita: the captain held on to the overturned boat with his one good hand
preguntas.explicacion: “Overturned” means turned upside down (es: volcado); the captain holds on to the overturned boat.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The water was warm when the men jumped into the sea.
preguntas.cita: The boat turned over as the men jumped into the sea. The water was like ice.
preguntas.explicacion: The water was freezing (“like ice”), not mild.

preguntas.pregunta: What did the captain do when the man on the shore came to help him?
opciones: He waved him away and sent him to the reporter.
He asked him to save the boat first.
He let the man pull him to the beach.
He swam to the beach on his own.
respuestas: He waved him away and sent him to the reporter.
preguntas.cita: But the captain waved him away and sent him to the reporter.
preguntas.explicacion: The captain refuses help and sends the rescuer towards the reporter. The text does not say that the captain reached the beach or that he asked for the boat to be saved.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The captain drowned before reaching the beach.
preguntas.explicacion: This adaptation does not say what happens to the captain: only that he refuses help and that the rescuer shouts “What's that?”. The text neither confirms nor rules out that he drowned.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: People on the beach brought the survivors blankets, clothes and drinks.
preguntas.cita: the beach was filled with men with blankets, clothes and whiskey. Women brought hot coffee.
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph 24 says that the beach filled with men carrying blankets, clothes and whisky, and that the women brought hot coffee.

tribunal.pregunta: Why didn't the men simply wait for help once they had been seen from the shore?
tribunal.pista_es: Comprehension: explain why help did not arrive and why they decided to act alone.
ideas: the signals from the shore were confusing
night fell and nobody came
they were growing weaker and feared they would not be able to swim

tribunal.pregunta: How does the author show the reporter's loneliness during the night?
tribunal.pista_es: Literary analysis: isolation, the shark, the wind and the poem.
ideas: he felt he was the only man afloat on all the oceans
the sad voice of the wind
the shark and his wish that the others would wake up
the memory of the poem about the dying soldier

tribunal.pregunta: What does the captain's behaviour at the end tell us about him?
tribunal.pista_es: Interpret the captain’s character: responsibility and sacrifice.
ideas: he gives orders until the end
he sends the rescuer to the reporter first
sense of duty towards the men under his command

tribunal.pregunta: Do you think the story is mainly about the power of nature or about human solidarity?
tribunal.pista_es: Reasoned opinion on the central theme of the story.
ideas: nature is indifferent and overwhelming
the men survive thanks to cooperation
the help of strangers on the beach

tribunal.pregunta: The text ends with a note about a lesson plan. Why might this story be useful for language learners?
tribunal.pista_es: Reflection on the educational use of literature and the strategy of predicting.
ideas: simple language with strong suspense
predicting what happens next improves comprehension
real events make the story engaging

tribunal.pregunta: In Spain, rescues at sea are frequent, for instance on the migratory routes to the Canary Islands. How should public authorities organise maritime rescue?
tribunal.pista_es: Link the text to current affairs in Spain: Salvamento Marítimo (maritime rescue service), the duty to assist and cooperation.
ideas: duty to rescue people in distress at sea
role of the Spanish maritime rescue service and coordination with the EU
funding and resources for search and rescue

tribunal.pregunta: Should the European Union share the cost of search and rescue operations among Member States? Why?
tribunal.pista_es: European policy debate: solidarity, common funding and Frontex.
ideas: frontline states bear a disproportionate burden
EU budget and agencies such as Frontex
solidarity mechanisms in the Pact on Migration and Asylum

moving toward the north · the cardinal compass point that is at 0 or 360 degrees

overcome by superior force · overcome, as with emotions or perceptual stimuli
